title: He Ignored a Dying King's Final Command... and It Changed Israel Forever
paragraphs:
He Ignored a Dying King's Final Command... and It Changed Israel Forever
The Tragic Story of Joab Shows That Yesterday's Loyalty Can Never Replace Today's Obedience
There are moments in Scripture that feel almost unbearable because they expose a truth we spend our lives trying to avoid.
This is one of them.
Imagine standing beside the bed of a king whose heartbeat is slowing with every passing breath.
This is not an ordinary man.
This is David.
The shepherd.
The giant slayer.
The sweet psalmist of Israel.
The king after God's own heart.
His victories are legendary.
His failures are public.
His repentance still echoes across generations.
Now his life is ending.
His final words are no longer about kingdoms, military victories, wealth, or fame.
He speaks about justice.
He speaks about unfinished obedience.
He speaks about Joab.
Not because Joab was David's greatest enemy.
But because he had once been one of David's closest companions.
Sometimes the deepest wounds never come from strangers.
They come from those who once fought beside us.
The account begins in 1 Kings 2:5–6, where David tells Solomon:

"Moreover thou knowest also what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, and what he did to the two captains of the hosts of Israel, unto Abner the son of Ner, and unto Amasa the son of Jether, whom he slew, and shed the blood of war in peace... Do therefore according to thy wisdom, and let not his hoar head go down to the grave in peace." (KJV)
At first glance, these words almost seem harsh.
Was David seeking revenge?
Had an old king become bitter?
The rest of Scripture answers with a firm no.
David had spared Saul.
He forgave Shimei.
He showed mercy to Mephibosheth.
David understood grace.
But grace never cancels justice.

The Hebrew word translated "blood" is דָּם (dām), meaning life itself poured out through violence. It carries covenant significance throughout the Old Testament. Joab did not merely kill men. He polluted the land with innocent blood.
God had already declared:
"So ye shall not pollute the land wherein ye are: for blood, it defileth the land." (Numbers 35:33)
Justice delayed does not become justice forgotten.
Joab had been loyal.
Remarkably loyal.
He fought beside David for decades.
He defended Israel countless times.
He won impossible battles.
If anyone looked like a faithful servant from the outside...
It was Joab.
Yet beneath his military brilliance lived a heart that increasingly obeyed his own wisdom instead of God's order.
Again and again, Joab crossed lines God never gave him permission to cross.
When Abner came seeking peace, Joab murdered him.
When Amasa was appointed commander, Joab embraced him with one hand...
and drove a sword into his stomach with the other.
The Hebrew narrative is chilling in its simplicity.
There is no dramatic speech.
Only betrayal.
Only blood.
Only silence.
Joab became dangerously convinced that because he often fought for David...
he could ignore David whenever it suited him.
That illusion still destroys believers today.
We convince ourselves that because we serve...
because we give...
because we attend church...
because we know Scripture...
God surely overlooks the areas where we quietly refuse Him.
But yesterday's faithfulness never licenses today's rebellion.
Perhaps Joab's greatest act of disobedience came years earlier.
David had given one of the clearest military commands in all Scripture concerning his son Absalom.
Twice the king publicly instructed every commander:
"Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom." (2 Samuel 18:5)
The Hebrew phrase is remarkably tender:
לְאַט־לִי לַנַּעַר (le'at-li la-na'ar)
Literally,
"Be gentle with the young man—for me."
Not because Absalom deserved it.
He certainly did not.
Absalom had rebelled.
Stolen hearts.
Started civil war.
Driven his own father from Jerusalem.
Yet David's heart remained a father's heart.
Joab heard the command.
He understood the command.
Then he deliberately ignored it.
When Absalom hung helplessly in the branches of the great oak, Joab took three spears and thrust them into Absalom's heart.
Then ten armor-bearers finished what Joab began.
It was victory.
But not obedience.
Many people celebrate results.
God examines obedience.
Joab believed he was protecting the kingdom.
God saw a man rejecting rightful authority.
There is a profound warning here.
Doing what seems practical is not always doing what is righteous.
The Hebrew word often translated "hear" or "obey" is שָׁמַע (shāmaʿ).
It means far more than listening.
It means hearing with the intention of obeying.
This is why Samuel declared:
"To obey is better than sacrifice." (1 Samuel 15:22)
The word translated "obey" is rooted in שָׁמַע (shāmaʿ).
God has never been impressed merely by activity.
He seeks surrendered hearts.
Years passed.
Joab appeared untouchable.
Consequences seemed absent.
Many people mistake delayed judgment for divine approval.
Scripture never does.
Eventually David died.
Solomon became king.
Adonijah attempted to seize the throne.
Joab sided with the wrong king.
Again.
Not because he lacked intelligence.
Because he refused submission.
When Solomon finally ordered Joab's execution, Joab fled to the Tabernacle and grasped the horns of the altar.
The altar represented mercy.
But mercy was never intended to become a hiding place for unrepentant rebellion.
Solomon ordered Benaiah to execute him there.
Joab died clinging to the symbol of grace...
without embracing the God of grace.
How many still do the same?
People cling to Christian identity.
To church attendance.
To religious routines.
To ministry.
To memories of what they once did for God.
Yet their hearts remain untouched by repentance.
Jesus addressed this tragedy with sobering clarity.
In Matthew 7:21, He declared:
"Not everyone who says to Me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of My Father."

The Greek word translated "does" is ποιῶν (poiōn), the present active participle of ποιέω (poieō), meaning "the one continually practicing" the Father's will. Genuine faith is not merely professed; it is lived in ongoing obedience.
Likewise, Jesus asked:
"Why do you call me, 'Lord, Lord,' and do not do what I tell you?" (Luke 6:46)
Love for Christ is measured not by emotion alone but by obedient trust.
Jesus said:
"If you love Me, keep My commandments." (John 14:15)

The Greek verb τηρήσετε (tērēsēte), from τηρέω (tēreō), means to guard, keep, watch over, or faithfully preserve. Obedience is not legalism; it is the loving response of those who treasure their Savior.
Joab's life is heartbreaking because it reminds us that someone can spend years close to God's work while remaining far from God's heart.
He fought for the right king...
yet often ignored the king's voice.
How close is that to many of us?
We sing.
We volunteer.
We post Bible verses.
We defend Christianity online.
We wear crosses.
We know theology.
Yet is there an area where Jesus keeps saying, "Be gentle," while we insist on vengeance?
An area where He says, "Forgive," while we choose bitterness?
An area where He says, "Trust Me," while we cling to control?
The gospel is not merely about avoiding judgment.
It is about receiving a new heart.
The prophet Ezekiel proclaimed God's promise:
"A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you..." (Ezekiel 36:26)
That promise reaches its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Unlike Joab, Jesus obeyed the Father's will perfectly.
Where Joab shed innocent blood, Jesus willingly shed His own innocent blood.
Where Joab grasped the altar hoping to escape justice, Jesus became the true sacrifice upon the altar, satisfying divine justice and extending mercy to all who repent and believe.
Isaiah foretold this glorious exchange:
"He was wounded for our transgressions, He was bruised for our iniquities... and with His stripes we are healed." (Isaiah 53:5)
The New Testament proclaims that this was fulfilled in Christ, whose death reconciles sinners to God through faith in Him alone (Romans 5:8–11; 2 Corinthians 5:21).
No failure is beyond His redemption.
No scandal is stronger than His cross.
No past is too broken for His resurrection power.
But grace is never permission to ignore the King's voice.
Grace transforms us into people who long to obey because we love the One who first loved us.
Maybe this story exposed something you were trying to hide.
Maybe you've been serving God outwardly while resisting Him inwardly.
Maybe you've been holding tightly to religion while quietly ignoring the gentle commands of Christ.
Today, the King still speaks.
His invitation is not condemnation.
It is repentance.
It is forgiveness.
It is restoration.
It is life.
If this message stirred your heart, don't let it end here.
Let it remind you that the King's voice is always worth following.
One act of obedience today may rewrite a story that generations after you will never forget.
